title: Silence as Communication
hook: Between men who know each other well, silence can carry more than talk: comfort, respect, anger, or a question nobody wants to ask out loud.
why:
Men are often accused of not talking, and sometimes the accusation is fair. But a great deal of what passes between men passes in silence: the hour on a riverbank without a word, the quiet in the car after a funeral, the silence that falls when a friend says something that matters and nobody knows what to say. There is also the other kind: the stony silence in an argument, the silent treatment that lasts for days, the silence of a man who has stopped trying to be heard.

The chapter on voice in Part I treated pauses as the sound of thinking. This chapter treats silence as a message in its own right. It covers what brief silences do to a group, how silence can comfort and why some cultures fall silent at exactly the moments others rush to talk, the comfortable silence of old friends, the stonewalling that damages relationships and why it often happens, the silent treatment as punishment, how to tell one silence from another, and how to hold a silence well.

teach.p:
In 2011 Namkje Koudenburg, Tom Postmes and Ernestine Gordijn asked people to imagine themselves in a conversation, or to watch a video of three people talking, in which the talk either flowed smoothly or was interrupted by a silence of just four seconds. People who experienced the silence reported feeling less self-assured, more rejected and less like they belonged, and some of them had not even noticed that it had happened.

The finding captures something everyone knows. A gap in conversation is felt before it is thought about. In a group, a brief silence after someone speaks can feel like a verdict on what they said. Koudenburg's later research found that when a group fell silent after someone expressed an opinion, people who badly wanted to belong tended to shift their opinion toward the group's.

But the meaning of a silence depends entirely on the setting and the relationship. The four-second gap that feels like rejection among new colleagues may feel like nothing at all between two old friends fishing, and like comfort between two men at a graveside. Silence is a blank that each person fills with what they expect.

That is why reading silence is so hard and so important. The figures here sit together on a bench, not speaking. Whether this is the easy quiet of friends, the tense quiet after an argument, or the heavy quiet of grief cannot be told from the silence itself. It has to be read from everything around it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if brief silences had no effect on how people felt about a conversation. Koudenburg and colleagues found that they did, though in imagined and watched conversations rather than live ones, so effects in real conversation may be weaker or stronger.

teach.p:
In 1970 the anthropologist Keith Basso described the situations in which Western Apache people in Arizona chose to say nothing. They kept silent on meeting strangers, in the early stages of courtship, when children returned home after a long absence, when someone was shouting at them in anger, when they were with people who were grieving, and during curing ceremonies. Basso's explanation was that silence was the proper response to situations in which relationships were uncertain or unpredictable. With a grieving person, words could wound, and the right thing was to be present and quiet.

Many Western men would recognise the instinct, even if their culture tells them that silence in such moments is awkward. A man sitting with a friend who has just lost his father often feels he should say something and has nothing to say. Basso's account suggests that the silence may itself be the right thing, provided it is a silence of presence rather than absence.

The difference shows in the body. A comforting silence stays near: it sits beside, looks at the same thing, breathes slowly, perhaps rests a hand on a shoulder. It does not check a phone, look at the door or fidget. It says I am here, and I am not going anywhere, without the risk of saying the wrong thing.

The figures here stand together, heads bowed, saying nothing. At a funeral, this is often the most eloquent thing three men can do. The chapter on mourning together at the end of this part returns to it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if silence in the presence of grief were always experienced as abandonment. For some grieving people it is, which is why a comforting silence must stay physically present and be broken when the other person wants to talk.

teach.p:
Among the clearest signs of a close friendship is the ability to be silent together without strain. Two old friends on a long walk may go twenty minutes without speaking, and both will describe it afterwards as a good walk. Two new acquaintances in the same silence would be searching for something to say within seconds.

You can usually tell the difference by watching. In a comfortable silence, bodies are relaxed and still. Breathing is slow and even. Both people tend to look at the same thing, or at nothing in particular, rather than at each other. When talk resumes, it does so easily, often on a new subject, with no sense of having rescued the moment.

In an awkward silence, the body works. People fidget, shift, touch their faces, glance at each other and away, check phones. Breathing becomes shallow. When talk resumes, it comes with a little burst of relief or a forced topic, and someone may laugh at nothing. Koudenburg's findings suggest why: an awkward silence feels like a threat to belonging, and the body treats it as one.

For a reader, the ease of a shared silence is a useful measure of a relationship. If you and a friend can no longer be quiet together without strain, something may have changed between you. The figures here walk side by side, in step, saying nothing. The rhythm of their walking does the talking.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the ease of shared silence bore no relation to how close two people were. The claim rests on observation and on research on conversational flow rather than on direct measurement of friends' silences, so treat it as a useful heuristic.

teach.p:
The psychologist John Gottman, who spent decades studying couples in conflict, identified stonewalling as one of four behaviours that predict the breakdown of a relationship. A stonewaller withdraws from the conversation: he goes silent, his face becomes still, he looks away or down, he stops giving the small nods and sounds that show he is listening. To the other person, he seems to have turned to stone, and it feels like contempt or indifference.

Gottman reported that in his studies, roughly 80 to 85 per cent of stonewallers were men. He also found that stonewalling often follows what he called flooding: a state of physical overwhelm during conflict, often marked by a heart rate above about 100 beats a minute, in which a person can no longer think clearly or listen. On this account, the stonewaller is not indifferent at all. He is overwhelmed, and silence is his attempt to stop the flood.

That does not make stonewalling harmless; it still leaves the other person shut out. But it changes the remedy. Gottman's advice is to recognise flooding, say so, and take a real break of at least twenty minutes, doing something calming rather than rehearsing the argument, before coming back to it. The chapter on disagreement later in this part builds on this.

The figure here has turned away, arms hanging, face hidden. In an argument, this posture is often read as I do not care. It may mean I cannot cope right now. Only he can tell you which, and he may need twenty minutes before he can.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if stonewalling were usually a calm, deliberate choice rather than a response to overwhelm. Gottman's observations support the flooding account, though his figures come from his own studies of couples rather than from independent replications.

teach.p:
There is another kind of silence that does deliberate harm. The silent treatment, refusing to speak to someone as a punishment, is a form of what psychologists call ostracism, and the psychologist Kipling Williams has spent a career showing how much it hurts.

In one of the best-known studies, published in 2000, Williams, Christopher Cheung and Wilma Choi had people play a simple online game of catch with two other players they would never meet. In one version, the other players simply stopped throwing the ball to them after a few throws. Even this trivial exclusion, by strangers, over a computer, lowered people's mood and their sense of belonging and control. The game, called Cyberball, has since been used in hundreds of studies with similar results.

If being left out of a game by strangers stings, being frozen out for days by a partner, a father or a friend hurts a great deal more. The silent treatment can feel safer to the person giving it than an argument, but to the person receiving it, it often feels like being erased.

It is worth distinguishing the silent treatment from needing space. Saying “I need an hour on my own, then I'll come and find you” is a silence with a door left open. Refusing to speak, with no explanation and no end in sight, is a silence with the door locked. The figures here stand turned away from each other. Whether this is a pause or a punishment depends on whether either of them has said when it will end.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if being ignored had little effect on people. The Cyberball research consistently finds that it does, though laboratory exclusion is far milder than the silent treatment in real relationships.

teach.p:
When a man falls silent, the question is which silence you are hearing. The rivals are many: comfort, thought, grief, fatigue, comfortable familiarity, disagreement held back, flooding, punishment, depression, or simply nothing to say. Reading them uses everything this book has covered.

Look at the breath: slow and even, held, or quick and shallow. Look at the posture: settled, braced, collapsed or turned away. Look at the face and gaze: relaxed and wandering, fixed on a point, avoiding you, or closed. Look at the hands: still, fidgeting, gripping. And look at what came before: a question he did not want to answer, a remark that stung, a long day, a piece of bad news.

Compare it with his baseline. Some men are naturally quiet, and their silence carries less than another man's. Some cultures place more value on silence in conversation than others, and some neurodivergent people find conversation tiring and need quiet to recover. A silence that is out of character is more informative than one that is not.

When in doubt, check lightly. “Quiet one tonight?” or “You've gone quiet; are you all right?” gives him an easy way to tell you, and an easy way to say he is fine. The figure here sits still, hands clasped in his lap. He might be calm, or holding himself very carefully together. His silence alone will not tell you which.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if different kinds of silence looked the same in the body. They often overlap, which is why the reading must draw on context and baseline and be checked with a question.

teach.p:
Holding a silence is a skill, and most people are poor at it. The commonest mistake is to fill it. A friend says something hard, and the listener rushes in with advice, reassurance or a story of his own, because the silence feels unbearable. The friend, who was perhaps about to say more, stops.

After you ask a real question, wait. Count slowly to ten in your head if you need to. Keep your body still and near, your breath slow, your eyes on something other than his face if you are side by side. Many men need the silence to find the words, and the words that come after it are often the important ones.

With grief, let the silence be company, and let him break it. With anger, give space, but say when you will be back, so that your silence is a pause rather than a punishment. In an argument, if you feel yourself flooding, say so before you go quiet: “I'm getting overwhelmed; I need twenty minutes, and then I want to finish this.”

And explain your own silences when they might be misread. “I'm quiet because I'm thinking about what you said, not because I'm annoyed” costs a sentence and prevents an hour of worry. The figures here sit side by side on a bench. One of the most generous things a man can do for another is to sit beside him in silence and not need it to end.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if filling silences helped people say difficult things. Experience in counselling and conversation research suggests the opposite, though some people find long silences uncomfortable and need a gentle prompt.
teach.pullQuote: Sit beside him in silence, and do not need it to end.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Reaching for a phone in a pause
poseGallery.annotation: A phone in a pause says that the silence is empty. Staying still and near says that it is shared.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Going silent and turning away mid-argument
poseGallery.annotation: Stonewalling shuts the other person out even when it is really overwhelm. Name it, take a real break, and come back.
A silence that punishes locks the door. A silence that keeps company leaves it open.

caseStudy:
Martin, fifty-two, and his wife Claire have the same argument every few months, about money. It goes the same way each time. Claire raises something, Martin answers briefly, Claire presses, and Martin goes silent. He sits very still, stares at the table, and stops responding. Claire reads it as contempt and gets louder. Eventually Martin leaves the room, and they do not speak for a day.

After one of these arguments, Claire shows Martin an article about stonewalling and flooding. He reads it twice. The description of his own experience, the pounding heart, the sense of being unable to think, the urge to shut down, is so exact that he is embarrassed. He had always thought of his silence as keeping the peace.

They agree on a signal. When Martin feels himself flooding, he will say, “I need twenty minutes,” go for a walk, and come back to finish the conversation. The first time, he comes back after forty minutes and apologises for the extra twenty. The conversation that follows is the best they have had about money in years.

That spring, Martin's father is dying in a hospice. Martin visits every evening and sits by the bed for an hour, mostly in silence, his hand on the blanket near his father's. His father, who never talked much either, sometimes opens his eyes and looks at him, and Martin nods.

At the funeral, his brother says that their father told the nurses those evenings were the best part of his day. Martin realises that he has known two very different silences his whole life, and has only lately learned to tell them apart.
observe: Notice the next silence in a group conversation, how long it lasts, and what people do with their bodies during it.
Notice which of your friends you can be silent with comfortably, and which you cannot.
Notice your own silences in disagreement: when you go quiet, what is happening in your body?
Notice a silence that someone explains, and one that nobody explains, and how each one feels.

drills.name: Count to Ten
steps: In your next real conversation, after you ask a question that matters, count slowly to ten in your head before saying anything else.
Keep your body still and your breathing slow while you count.
Notice whether the other person fills the silence, and what they say.
Afterwards, write down what came after the silence.

drills.name: Flooding Map
steps: Recall the last time you went silent in an argument.
Write down what was happening in your body: heart, breath, face, hands, thoughts.
Write down how the other person read your silence, if you know.
Write the sentence you could have said instead, such as “I need twenty minutes, then I want to finish this.”
Decide what you would do in those twenty minutes that would actually calm you.

drills.name: Silent Company
steps: Spend twenty minutes with a friend or family member doing something side by side in silence: a walk, a drive, fishing, a job.
Agree beforehand, if it helps, that you do not need to talk.
Notice the moments when you feel the urge to fill the silence, and what your body does.
Afterwards, ask how it was for the other person.
Write down whether the silence felt comfortable, awkward or something else.

drills.name: Explain a Silence
steps: For one week, whenever you go quiet in a way that might be misread, explain it in a sentence.
Use simple words, such as “I'm quiet because I'm thinking, not because I'm cross.”
Notice how people respond to the explanation.
At the end of the week, note whether any misunderstandings were avoided.

quiz.q: During an argument, a man goes silent, stares at the table and stops responding. What does Gottman's research suggest is often going on?
options: He has stopped caring about the relationship and is showing it
He is calmly deciding how best to win the argument when he speaks
He may be physically overwhelmed and shutting down to cope
He is waiting politely for his partner to finish what she has to say
quiz.explain: Gottman found that stonewalling often follows flooding, a state of physical overwhelm in which listening becomes hard. It still shuts the other person out, but the remedy is a real break and a return, not a judgment of indifference.

quiz.q: What did Koudenburg and colleagues find about a four-second silence in a conversation?
options: People felt more rejected and less as if they belonged, even unnoticed
People felt more relaxed, because the silence gave them time to think
The silence had no effect unless it lasted at least half a minute
Only people who noticed the silence were affected by it at all
quiz.explain: A brief disruption to the flow of conversation left people feeling less self-assured and more rejected, even when they had not noticed it. A silence is felt before it is thought about.

quiz.q: According to Keith Basso, when did Western Apache people tend to fall silent?
options: Only when they were angry with someone and wished to punish that person by withholding speech
In uncertain situations, such as meeting strangers or being with the grieving
Whenever they were speaking with someone older or more senior
Only during formal religious ceremonies, never in daily life
quiz.explain: Basso described silence as the proper response to situations where relationships were uncertain, including meeting strangers and being with people in grief. In those moments, silence was a form of respect and presence.

quiz.q: A man feels himself flooding during a row. What does Gottman's advice suggest he do?
options: Push through and keep talking until the whole argument is resolved, however long it takes
Go quiet and leave the room, then avoid the subject in future
Raise his voice, so that the other person stops and listens to him
Say he is overwhelmed, take a break of twenty minutes or more, then return
quiz.explain: Naming the flooding, taking a real break that is actually calming, and coming back to finish the conversation turns a stonewall into a pause. Leaving with no return turns it into the silent treatment.

quiz.q: What did the Cyberball studies show about being ignored?
options: Even brief exclusion by strangers in a game lowered mood and belonging
People felt nothing when ignored, as long as the others were strangers
Being left out of the game raised people's self-esteem, oddly enough
Exclusion only hurt when it came from close friends or family members
quiz.explain: Being left out of a simple online game of catch by strangers was enough to lower mood and sense of belonging. The silent treatment from someone close is a far stronger version of the same harm.

quiz.q: You ask a friend how he is coping since his divorce. He goes quiet and looks out of the window. What fits this chapter best?
options: Fill the silence quickly with reassurance, so that he is not uncomfortable
Change the subject at once, since the silence shows he does not want to talk
Stay near and still, and wait, giving him time to find the words
Ask him three more questions in a row, so that he has to answer one of them
quiz.explain: Silence after a real question is often the time a man needs to find his words. Staying near and patient lets the next sentence come, and he can still choose not to answer.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific silence in your life that mattered: a silence that comforted you, one you used to shut someone out, or one that someone used on you. Describe the setting, what the bodies were doing, and how long it lasted. What did the silence mean to each person, and did they read it the same way? If it was a silence you created, what would you say now to make its meaning clear?
reflection.guidance: Silences are easy to remember by their feeling and hard to remember by their details, so try to recall the posture, breath, gaze and hands. If the silence was a stonewall or a silent treatment, be honest about what was happening in your body at the time. The point is not to judge yourself but to learn which silences you use, and how they land.

failureMode: The first failure is to treat silence as empty, when even a four-second gap can make people feel rejected. The second is to fill every silence, rushing in with advice or stories just as a man was about to say what mattered. The third is to read a stonewall as contempt without considering flooding, or, if you are the one stonewalling, to leave the other person shut out without naming what is happening and coming back. The fourth is to use silence as punishment, freezing someone out with no explanation and no end, which research on ostracism shows does real harm. And the fifth is to leave a grieving friend alone because you have nothing to say, when your silent presence would have been enough.
